title: The teaching of all Buddhas (183–187)
hookLine: not to do any evil, to do good, to purify one's mind: this is the teaching of the awakened (Dhammapada 183)

lines: A LINE SAID IN ONE BREATH.
cards: Could you sum up everything you believe in one sentence? Most of us would ramble, or give a slogan we don't quite live by. Some traditions have a short answer ready, a line people can say in one breath.

In Buddhism, today's verse is that kind of line: this, it says, is the teaching of all the Awakened. It's short enough to memorize by the end of today. And it's so hard that, the story goes, an old man can't manage it.

teach.b: Verse one eighty-three, in Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Three movements. Avoid harm.
Do good. Purify the mind. The first two are about what you do.
The third turns inward: in this verse, it isn't enough to behave well; the mind behind the behavior has to be cleared, of greed, of hatred, of confusion. That's what sitting is for.
Tradition holds that this verse, with the two after it, was spoken on a full-moon day to twelve hundred fifty awakened disciples who gathered without being called.
Remember Magha Puja, from camp three? This is the teaching that holy day remembers. Verse one eighty-four adds the spirit of it: "The Awakened call patience the highest penance."
Not dramatic self-punishment. Patience. Verse one eighty-five lists small, practical pieces: "Not to blame, not to strike," to eat in moderation, to sit in solitude, to dwell on the highest thoughts.
People in China tell a story about this verse. A well-known poet-official climbed to meet a Chan master who lived in a tree, and asked for the essence of Buddhism. The master gave him this verse.

teach.h: A CHILD OF THREE KNOWS IT.
teach.b: The poet laughed: a child of three knows that.
The master answered: a child of three may know it, but an old man of eighty can't do it. The teaching is simple enough to say, and big enough for a lifetime.

how: Verses 183–185, known as the Ovāda Pāṭimokkha, are chanted in Theravada monasteries, and many Buddhists commemorate their teaching on Magha Puja, the full moon of the third lunar month.

games.q: match each piece of the teaching.

s: verse 183 is only about outward behavior
its third part is purifying the mind behind the behavior.
verse 184 calls patience the highest penance
"the Awakened call patience the highest penance": not self-punishment, patience.
in the story, the Chan master agreed the verse was too simple
he said a child of three may know it, but an old man of eighty can't do it.

games.q: a well-known poet asks a master for the essence of Buddhism, and hears: avoid harm, do good, purify the mind. the poet laughs: a child of three knows that! what does the master say?
o: then you're ready to be a monk.
a child may know it; an old man of eighty can't do it.
then I'll give you something harder.
games.why: the teaching is simple to say and takes a lifetime to do. that's a story people tell in China, not from the Pali texts.

practice: Avoid: is there one small harm, a jab, a shortcut, a bite of gossip, you can simply not do today? Do: is there one small good, a greeting, a thank-you, a helping hand, you can add?
Purify: that one happens right here, as the breath settles the mind and each flicker of irritation or wanting is noticed and let pass, like dust settling in a glass of water.

wordCard.voice: Sāsana, the Pali word for teaching: verse one eighty-three says not to do any harm, to do good, to purify one's own mind.

orig.note: Pali: teaching, instruction — as in etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ, this is the teaching of the Buddhas.

carryVoice: Your line: avoid, do, purify. The whole teaching of the Buddhas fits on three fingers. Until tomorrow.
